bib.title: Clean Code, Chapter 10: Classes (with Jeff Langr)
bib.venue: Prentice Hall (Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship), pp. 135-151

question: How should classes be sized, organised and isolated so that code stays clean above the level of functions?

results.claim: Class size is measured by counting responsibilities, not lines.
results.setup: Java OO design guidance; contrast with functions, which are measured in physical lines.

results.claim: A class description should fit in about 25 words without 'if', 'and', 'or' or 'but'; otherwise the class has too many responsibilities.
results.setup: Heuristic test for class size, applied to SuperDashboard (Listings 10-1, 10-2).
results.quote: a brief description of the class in about 25 words

results.claim: A class with only five public methods can still be too big if it has two reasons to change (version info and Swing component management).
results.setup: SuperDashboard extends JFrame; Listing 10-2 versus Listing 10-1.
results.quote: Five methods isn’t too much, is it? In this case it is because despite its small number

results.claim: SRP: a class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change.
results.source: Martin, Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices (2002) [PPP]
results.setup: Stated as definition of responsibility and guideline for class size.
results.quote: states that a class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change

results.claim: Many small classes have no more moving parts than a few large ones; the chapter answers the fear that small classes obscure the big picture with a toolbox analogy.
results.setup: Argument against developers who fear navigating many classes.
results.quote: a system with many small classes has no more moving parts than a system

results.claim: Cohesion is judged by how many instance variables each method uses; classes should have few instance variables.
results.setup: Stack (Listing 10-4): of three methods only size() fails to use both variables.
results.quote: A class in which each variable is used by each method is maximally cohesive.

results.claim: Variables used by only a subset of methods signal a hidden class; promoting local variables to instance variables to shorten parameter lists erodes cohesion, so split the class.
results.quote: When classes lose cohesion, split them!

results.claim: Refactoring PrintPrimes (Knuth) into three classes grew the program from a little over one page to nearly three pages, due to longer names, declarations as commentary and whitespace.
results.source: Knuth, Literate Programming (1992), WEB output translated to Java
results.note: Quote kept short: the sentence continues across a line break, 'a little over one page to nearly three pages in length'.

results.claim: The refactoring was done by writing a test suite that verified the first program, then making many tiny changes, running the program after each; it was not a rewrite and kept the same algorithm.
A class that must be opened to add a statement type (Sql) violates SRP; split each statement into a subclass so adding UpdateSql changes no existing class (OCP).
results.setup: Listings 10-9 and 10-10, Sql class generating SQL strings.
results.quote: Classes should be open for extension but closed for modiﬁcation.
results.note: The source text contains the 'fi' ligature in 'modification'.

results.claim: Action should be spurred by actual change: if the class is logically complete and no update support is foreseeable, leave it alone.
results.note: Text hyphenated across lines: 'the primary spur for taking action should be system change itself'. Next: 'as soon as we find ourselves opening up a class, we should consider fixing our design'.

results.claim: Depending on an interface instead of a concrete API (Portfolio takes a StockExchange) makes tests deterministic: a stub fixing MSFT at 100 gives a 500 total for five shares.
results.setup: PortfolioTest with FixedStockExchangeStub; TokyoStockExchange API is volatile.

results.claim: DIP in essence: classes should depend upon abstractions, not on concrete details.
results.quote: our classes should depend upon abstractions, not on concrete details

results.claim: Class layout: public static constants, private static variables, private instance variables, public functions, with private utilities directly after the public function that calls them (stepdown rule).
results.quote: There is seldom a good reason to have a public variable.

results.claim: Encapsulation may be loosened to protected or package scope so a test can reach a member, but only as a last resort.
results.setup: Java; tests in the same package.

limits: No data or measurement: all claims are assertions or hand-picked Java examples.
Written for Java in 2008; recompilation and package-scope arguments do not carry over to Python.
Authors concede the rules are not absolute: they are 'not fanatic' about privacy and say maximally cohesive classes are neither advisable nor possible.
SRP is framed here as 'one reason to change'; the later 'one group of people' framing (2014) is not in this chapter.
practices: Order a class: constants, static vars, instance vars, public functions, each followed by the private helpers it calls (p. 136).
Keep variables and utilities private; loosen to protected or package scope for tests only as a last resort (p. 136).
Size classes by responsibilities; the first rule is small, the second is smaller (p. 136).
If a concise name cannot be found, or the name has Processor, Manager or Super in it, suspect too many responsibilities (p. 138).
Describe the class in about 25 words without if, and, or, but (p. 138).
Give each class one reason to change; extract groups of methods such as Version (pp. 138-139).
After the program works, go back and split overstuffed classes (p. 139).
Keep cohesion high; when subsets of methods share instance variables, split them into a new class (pp. 140-141).
Refactor under a test suite in tiny steps, running after each (p. 146).
Restructure so new features are added by extension (subclass) not modification: OCP (p. 149).
Spot SRP violations by private methods that serve only a subset of the class, but act when change arrives (p. 147).
Depend on interfaces; inject them through the constructor so tests can supply stubs: DIP (pp. 149-150).

terms.definition: a class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change
Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification
our classes should depend upon abstractions, not on concrete details
A class in which each variable is used by each method is maximally cohesive; high cohesion means methods and variables are co-dependent and hang together as a logical whole
A class like SuperDashboard exposing about 70 public methods
